files.title: Context file
files.body:
# AGENTS.md — {{initiative}}

> Node SDLC · Act II PLAN · Scale: Solo / small. Read this first, every session.

## How we work
People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.
- **You:** Choose what to work on · give context · make decisions · review and correct · sign off · own the artifact
- **Your agent:** Draft · research · summarise · structure into templates · spot gaps and risks · check against criteria · prepare options

## Where this act sits
PLAN is part of the **Discovery track** — Are we building the right thing? The acts keep their order as a logical dependency — a problem is validated before it is planned, designed before it is built — but they are kinds of work that run continuously and in parallel, at different sizes, not phases on a calendar.

## PLAN: Turn a validated opportunity into a scoped, prioritised, estimated, sequenced and funded commitment that DESIGN can start on.
- **2.1 Requirements Engineering** — gate: Requirements Baseline. Produces: Outcome & success-criteria map, Business requirements specification, Stakeholder needs register, Requirements specification, Traceability matrix, Requirements baseline.
- **2.2 Scope & Prioritisation** — gate: Scope Agreement. Produces: Scope statement, Story map, Initiative breakdown, Slice plan, WSJF scoring sheet, Product backlog.
- **2.3 Estimation & Capacity** — gate: Forecast Agreed. Produces: Estimate sheet, Capacity plan, Delivery forecast, Scope–time–capacity trade-off.
- **2.4 Roadmap & Release Planning** — gate: Roadmap Agreed. Produces: Dependency register, Release roadmap, Release plan, Roadmap briefing.
- **2.5 Investment & Approval** — gate: Commitment. Produces: Business case, Funding confirmation, Commitment conditions, Commitment decision record, Committed initiative pack, Learning log, PLAN retrospective.
- Act gate: **Commitment** — decided by: Sponsor commits within their limit; portfolio board above it and on escalation..

## Conventions
- Artifacts live in `docs/<artifact>.md`, written from `templates/<artifact>.md`.
- Every artifact carries its trace ID and links the IDs upstream of it; register new IDs in `TRACE.md`.
- Trace chain: NEED → RQ → EPC → FEA → EST → RMP → BC → CMT → LRN.
- Log each step in `PROGRESS.md`.
- Before saving, score the artifact against `rubrics/<artifact>.md`.

## Your toolkit
- `commands/` — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act. Start with `plan-run-act` or the unit you're on.
- `workflows/` — run specs with checkpoints; stop at every checkpoint.
- `skills/` — how-to packages for each technique; load the ones a command names.
- `agents/` — reviewers by lens, plus researcher, synthesiser, challenger and decision-brief writer.
- `TOOLS.md` and `GUARDRAILS.md` — what you may use and must never do.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

## Scale: Solo / small
I play all the roles. Keep every output short (one page or one screen), merge steps where it makes sense, and skip formal sign-offs — but keep the decision record and the learning log.
Access: Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.

files.title: Accessibility reviewer
files.body:
---
name: accessibility-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Accessibility lens — Usable by people with disabilities; WCAG. Use after: 2.1.2.1 S2 Run workshops & interviews; 2.1.3.1 S3 Quantify NFRs per quality attribute."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Accessibility reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at access for people with disabilities: conformance with WCAG and support for assistive technologies.

## Questions to ask
- Can people with disabilities use it?
- Did research include them?
- Which accessibility standard applies?

## Concerns to check
- Excluding users
- Legal exposure

## Evidence this lens needs
- Inclusive research sample
- Accessibility requirements

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.2.1 S2 Run workshops & interviews: Ask about clerks using screen magnifiers or keyboard only.
- 2.1.3.1 S3 Quantify NFRs per quality attribute: Highlighting distinguishable without colour alone.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: AI / ML reviewer
files.body:
---
name: ai-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the AI / ML lens — Model fitness, evaluation, drift, bias, oversight. Use after: 2.1.3.1 S3 Quantify NFRs per quality attribute; 2.2.3.1 S4 Every slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small?; 2.3.1.1 S5 Flag uncertainty & record EST-##; 2.3.2.1 S4 Allocation confirmed & gaps covered?."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the AI / ML reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the use of AI and machine learning: whether a model is fit for purpose, how it's evaluated, and how bias, drift and human oversight are handled.

## Questions to ask
- Is AI actually needed here?
- How will we evaluate model quality?
- What happens when it's wrong?
- Where is human oversight?

## Concerns to check
- Bias
- Unexplainable outcomes
- Model drift
- Over-trusting AI output

## Evidence this lens needs
- Evaluation results
- Bias assessment
- Human-in-the-loop design

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.3.1 S3 Quantify NFRs per quality attribute: Extraction accuracy measured on a labelled test set, including poor scans.
- 2.2.3.1 S4 Every slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small?: Parsing-accuracy risk retired by an early slice.
- 2.3.1.1 S5 Flag uncertainty & record EST-##: Parsing work flagged high-uncertainty until spiked.
- 2.3.2.1 S4 Allocation confirmed & gaps covered?: Is the ML-capable engineer actually booked?
- 2.5.3.1 S3 Run vendor due diligence: Vendor model accuracy claims verified.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Architecture reviewer
files.body:
---
name: architecture-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Architecture lens — Structure, quality attributes, hard-to-reverse trade-offs. Use after: 2.1.3.1 S4 Separate constraints & merge duplicates; 2.2.2.1 S2 Split epics into features; 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton; 2.3.1.1 S3 Size later items by T-shirt."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Architecture reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at structure and quality attributes: how the solution fits the existing landscape and which decisions will be expensive to reverse.

## Questions to ask
- How does this fit our current systems?
- Which quality attributes matter most?
- Which decisions are hard to reverse?
- What integration and data impacts are there?

## Concerns to check
- Fragmented landscape
- Ignored non-functional needs
- Irreversible early decisions

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state map
- Quality attribute priorities
- Architecture review notes

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.3.1 S4 Separate constraints & merge duplicates: ERP import API only stays a constraint, not a requirement.
- 2.2.2.1 S2 Split epics into features: Features by capability, not by component.
- 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton: Skeleton proves the integration path.
- 2.3.1.1 S3 Size later items by T-shirt: Coarse sizes flag architectural unknowns.
- 2.5.4.1 S2 Run the commitment meeting: Design questions for DESIGN listed.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Business / Strategy reviewer
files.body:
---
name: business-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Business / Strategy lens — Strategic fit, value hypothesis, opportunity cost. Use after: 2.1.1.1 S1 Read the brief & conditions aloud; 2.1.1.1 S5 Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?; 2.2.1.1 S3 List in / out / later with reasons; 2.2.4.1 S1 Score cost of delay as a group."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Business / Strategy reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the work through the organisation's strategy: does this move a goal that matters, is it worth more than the alternatives we're giving up, and does it fit how the business creates value?

## Questions to ask
- Which strategic goal or OKR does this move?
- What's the value hypothesis — and how will we know?
- What are we not doing if we do this (opportunity cost)?
- Why now?

## Concerns to check
- Pet projects with no strategic link
- Value claimed but never measured
- Strategy drift

## Evidence this lens needs
- Linked goals / OKRs
- Value hypothesis with a measure
- Opportunity size

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.1.1 S1 Read the brief & conditions aloud: Re-read the decision's conditions — they bind the plan.
- 2.1.1.1 S5 Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?: Two to four criteria the sponsor will be judged on.
- 2.2.1.1 S3 List in / out / later with reasons: Every out item has a reason the sponsor accepts.
- 2.2.4.1 S1 Score cost of delay as a group: Business value tied to outcomes.
- 2.2.4.1 S4 Order agreed by sponsor & product owner?: Order defended with scores, not seniority.
- 2.3.4.1 S3 Sponsor chooses an option that fits?: Sponsor chooses explicitly.
- 2.3.4.1 S4 Record the trade-off: Rejected options and why.
- 2.4.2.1 S1 Group features into outcome themes: Themes are outcomes.
- 2.4.4.1 S3 Objections resolved?: Objections resolved by the sponsor, not around them.
- 2.5.1.1 S1 Appraise options incl. do nothing: Do nothing is an option.
- 2.5.1.1 S6 Write the business case: Case states the benefit owner.
- 2.5.2.1 S1 Split into evidence-gated tranches: Tranche 2 gated on pilot results.
- 2.5.4.1 S3 Go / Phase / Rework / Escalate / No-go?: Go, Phase, Rework, Escalate or No-go — explicitly.
- 2.5.4.2 S4 Set revisit trigger & owner: Trigger tied to a date or measurable condition.
- 2.5.4.2 S5 Update the portfolio register: Portfolio status matches the decision.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Challenger
files.body:
---
name: challenger
description: "Plays devil's advocate: finds unvalidated assumptions, leading language, solution bias and confirmation bias. Use at: 2.1.1.1 S5 Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?; 2.1.2.1 S5 Each group recognises its needs?; 2.1.3.1 S5 Passes the 29148 quality check?; 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the challenger helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- List every assumption the work relies on and whether it has evidence.
- Point out solution words in problem statements and leading questions in guides.
- Ask the question the team is avoiding.
- Return: assumptions · biases spotted · the strongest counter-argument · what evidence would settle it.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

---

description: "Reviews work through the Compliance / Regulatory lens — Obligations and the evidence that proves them. Use after: 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?; 2.5.3.1 S2 Screen privacy, security & compliance; 2.5.4.1 S4 Record decision & conditions."

You are the Compliance / Regulatory reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at obligations from regulators and certifications, and the evidence needed to show they're met.

## Questions to ask
- Which regulations or certifications apply?
- What do they require of this solution?
- What evidence will auditors expect?
- Are there hard blockers?

## Concerns to check
- Discovering a regulatory blocker late
- Missing audit evidence

## Evidence this lens needs
- List of applicable obligations
- Compliance review notes

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?: Regulatory requirements included and traced.
- 2.5.3.1 S2 Screen privacy, security & compliance: Regulatory obligations listed.
- 2.5.4.1 S4 Record decision & conditions: Compliance conditions recorded.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Customer / User reviewer
files.body:
---
name: customer-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Customer / User lens — Real users, their jobs, and what adoption requires. Use after: 2.1.1.1 S2 Split the objective into outcomes; 2.1.2.1 S2 Run workshops & interviews; 2.1.4.1 S2 Walk stakeholders through scenarios; 2.1.4.2 S5 Notify affected owners."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Customer / User reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the work from the point of view of the people who will use it or be affected by it: their jobs, pains, contexts and what adoption would really take.

## Questions to ask
- Who exactly are the users, and in which situations?
- What job are they trying to get done?
- What do they do today instead?
- What would make them switch — or refuse?

## Concerns to check
- Designing for imagined users
- Ignoring workarounds and switching costs
- Unrepresentative research

## Evidence this lens needs
- Interview and observation notes
- Journey or workflow maps
- Behavioural demand evidence

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.1.1 S2 Split the objective into outcomes: Name whose experience changes.
- 2.1.2.1 S2 Run workshops & interviews: Hear the clerks in their own words.
- 2.1.4.1 S2 Walk stakeholders through scenarios: Stakeholders recognise their needs in scenarios.
- 2.1.4.2 S5 Notify affected owners: Stakeholders whose needs changed are told.
- 2.2.1.1 S1 Map the journey as a story map: Map the clerk's real journey, email to ERP.
- 2.2.4.1 S1 Score cost of delay as a group: User value scored from evidence.
- 2.3.4.1 S2 Generate & cost options: Which users lose what under each option.
- 2.4.2.1 S2 Place items in now / next / later: Users see value early.
- 2.4.4.1 S1 Tailor views per audience: A view users understand.
- 2.5.1.1 S1 Appraise options incl. do nothing: Option effects on users.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Data reviewer
files.body:
---
name: data-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Data lens — Models, lineage, quality, retention, migration. Use after: 2.1.1.1 S3 Pull baselines & set criteria; 2.1.3.1 S2 Classify into the four classes; 2.2.2.1 S3 Write a brief per feature; 2.5.3.1 S2 Screen privacy, security & compliance."

You are the Data reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at data: what's available, its quality and lineage, what new data is needed and how it is kept, migrated and used.

## Questions to ask
- What data exists, and is it trustworthy?
- What new data will we need?
- How will we measure outcomes?
- Who owns the data?

## Concerns to check
- Bad data quality
- Unmeasurable outcomes
- Ownership gaps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Data sources and owners
- Baselines
- Analytics plan

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.1.1 S3 Pull baselines & set criteria: Baseline from ERP timestamps, not from estimates.
- 2.1.3.1 S2 Classify into the four classes: Name the data each requirement reads and writes.
- 2.2.2.1 S3 Write a brief per feature: Note the data each feature touches.
- 2.5.3.1 S2 Screen privacy, security & compliance: Retention of PDFs and extracted data.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Decision-brief writer
files.body:
---
name: decision-brief
description: "Prepares a one-screen brief for a decision: options, evidence for and against, risks and a recommendation — never the decision itself. Use at: 2.1.1.1 S5 Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?; 2.1.2.1 S5 Each group recognises its needs?; 2.1.3.1 S5 Passes the 29148 quality check?; 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the decision-brief writer helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- Restate the decision in one line and who makes it.
- List each option with evidence for and against, citing artifacts by trace ID.
- Name the main risks of each option.
- Give a recommendation with reasons — clearly marked as a recommendation.
- Never make, imply or record the decision.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: DevOps / Delivery reviewer
files.body:
---
name: devops-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the DevOps / Delivery lens — Pipelines, flow, deployment safety. Use after: 2.2.2.1 S5 All covered, no orphans, no layers?; 2.2.3.1 S5 Order slices to retire risk early; 2.3.1.1 S2 Size slices with Planning Poker; 2.3.2.1 S3 Read historic throughput."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the DevOps / Delivery reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the delivery pipeline: flow, automation and deployment safety.

## Questions to ask
- Can we deliver this incrementally?
- What pipeline changes are needed?

## Concerns to check
- Big-bang delivery

## Evidence this lens needs
- Delivery approach

## In this act, look for
- 2.2.2.1 S5 All covered, no orphans, no layers?: Each feature can be delivered and released independently.
- 2.2.3.1 S5 Order slices to retire risk early: Slices fit inside a sprint.
- 2.3.1.1 S2 Size slices with Planning Poker: Include testing and deployment in every size.
- 2.3.2.1 S3 Read historic throughput: Throughput, not hours.
- 2.3.3.1 S4 Inputs and assumptions sound?: Inputs reviewed by the team.
- 2.4.1.1 S2 Add calendar constraints: Freeze windows and release calendar.
- 2.4.1.1 S5 Publish the register: Register reviewed weekly.
- 2.4.2.1 S3 Overlay dependencies & forecast: Now horizon fits the forecast.
- 2.4.3.1 S3 Plan rollout by site with criteria: Feature flag per site.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Domain / Business Process reviewer
files.body:
---
name: domain-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Domain / Business Process lens — Business rules, process flows, vocabulary, invariants. Use after: 2.1.2.1 S1 Plan elicitation per group; 2.1.2.1 S5 Each group recognises its needs?; 2.2.1.1 S1 Map the journey as a story map; 2.4.3.1 S3 Plan rollout by site with criteria."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Domain / Business Process reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the business domain itself: the processes, rules, vocabulary and invariants the software must respect.

## Questions to ask
- What are the real business processes and rules here?
- What words does the business use, and what do they mean?
- Which rules can never be broken?
- Where do processes cross teams or systems?

## Concerns to check
- Software that breaks business rules
- Misunderstood vocabulary
- Hidden process steps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state process / system map
- Domain rules list
- Glossary

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.2.1 S1 Plan elicitation per group: Cover every site — they handle orders differently.
- 2.1.2.1 S5 Each group recognises its needs?: Each group recognises its own needs.
- 2.2.1.1 S1 Map the journey as a story map: Include exceptions — unknown customers, partial orders.
- 2.4.3.1 S3 Plan rollout by site with criteria: Site readiness and local practice.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Engineering reviewer
files.body:
---
name: engineering-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Engineering lens — Implementability, code quality, maintainability. Use after: 2.1.3.1 S2 Classify into the four classes; 2.2.1.1 S2 Draw the MVP line; 2.2.2.1 S5 All covered, no orphans, no layers?; 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Engineering reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at implementability: can it be built and maintained with our technology, skills and time, at sustainable quality?

## Questions to ask
- Can we build this with what we have?
- What are the technical unknowns?
- What will it cost to maintain?
- What skills are missing?

## Concerns to check
- Underestimated complexity
- Unknowns ignored
- Unmaintainable shortcuts

## Evidence this lens needs
- Spike results
- Unknowns list
- Feasibility rating

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.3.1 S2 Classify into the four classes: No implementation in requirement text.
- 2.2.1.1 S2 Draw the MVP line: Thin but end to end.
- 2.2.2.1 S5 All covered, no orphans, no layers?: No layer-shaped features.
- 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton: Skeleton runs email → ERP draft at one site.
- 2.2.4.1 S3 Adjust for dependencies & enablers: Enablers ranked by the risk they retire.
- 2.3.1.1 S1 Agree reference items: Reference items the whole team knows.
- 2.3.1.1 S4 Estimates converged?: Divergence is information — discuss it.
- 2.3.2.1 S1 List people & allocation: Named people, real allocation.
- 2.3.2.1 S5 Publish the capacity range: Capacity published as a range.
- 2.3.3.1 S2 Simulate throughput (Monte Carlo): Throughput from history, not hope.
- 2.3.4.1 S1 Compare forecast with targets: Show the honest gap.
- 2.3.4.1 S5 Update backlog & re-forecast: Forecast re-run on the new scope.
- 2.4.1.1 S1 List dependencies per feature: Internal dependencies per feature.
- 2.5.2.1 S3 Confirm budget line & team: Team released by line managers.
- 2.5.4.1 S1 Assemble the commitment pack: Forecast and capacity in the pack.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Finance / Commercial reviewer
files.body:
---
name: finance-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Finance / Commercial lens — Cost, funding, pricing, unit economics, return. Use after: 2.1.1.1 S3 Pull baselines & set criteria; 2.2.1.1 S3 List in / out / later with reasons; 2.2.4.1 S1 Score cost of delay as a group; 2.3.2.1 S1 List people & allocation."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Finance / Commercial reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at money: cost, funding, pricing, unit economics and the return the initiative must justify.

## Questions to ask
- What will it cost — to build and to run?
- What is the return, and over what period?
- How is it funded, and is that within limits?
- What does a unit of value cost and earn?

## Concerns to check
- Hidden run costs
- Optimistic benefits
- Unfunded commitments

## Evidence this lens needs
- Cost range including run cost
- Opportunity size
- Business case

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.1.1 S3 Pull baselines & set criteria: Benefit maths uses the same baseline finance will use.
- 2.2.1.1 S3 List in / out / later with reasons: Price each addition the sponsor asks for.
- 2.2.4.1 S1 Score cost of delay as a group: Cost of delay in money where possible.
- 2.3.2.1 S1 List people & allocation: Contractor and licence costs noted.
- 2.3.3.1 S3 Read 50% / 85% dates & assumptions: Dates feed the cost model.
- 2.3.4.1 S2 Generate & cost options: Cost of each option.
- 2.4.2.1 S5 Assign RMP IDs & confidence: Roadmap items map to benefit ramp-up.
- 2.5.1.1 S2 Model benefits with ramp-up: Benefits with ramp-up by site.
- 2.5.1.1 S3 Model costs; compute NPV & payback: NPV and payback as ranges.
- 2.5.1.1 S5 Finance validates the model?: Finance signs the model.
- 2.5.2.1 S1 Split into evidence-gated tranches: Tranches tied to evidence milestones.
- 2.5.2.1 S2 Prepare the funding request: Request names budget line and amount.
- 2.5.4.1 S1 Assemble the commitment pack: Case, funding and tranche plan in the pack.
- 2.5.4.2 S2 Run the PLAN retrospective: Estimate and case accuracy to check in EVOLVE.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Governance / Risk reviewer
files.body:
---
name: governance-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Governance / Risk lens — Decision rights, risk appetite, auditable controls. Use after: 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?; 2.1.4.2 S3 Accept, defer or reject?; 2.2.4.1 S3 Adjust for dependencies & enablers; 2.3.3.1 S4 Inputs and assumptions sound?."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Governance / Risk reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at decision rights, risk appetite and controls: who may decide what, and whether there's an auditable trail from decision to evidence.

## Questions to ask
- Who has authority to decide?
- Is the risk within appetite?
- Is the decision recorded with its evidence?
- What must be escalated?

## Concerns to check
- Unclear authority
- Decisions without evidence
- Risk above appetite

## Evidence this lens needs
- RACI
- Risk register
- Decision record

## In this act, look for
- 2.1.4.1 S4 Complete enough for the now horizon?: No unowned TBD on a now-horizon item.
- 2.1.4.2 S3 Accept, defer or reject?: Beyond tolerance goes to the sponsor.
- 2.2.4.1 S3 Adjust for dependencies & enablers: Dependencies respected.
- 2.3.3.1 S4 Inputs and assumptions sound?: Assumptions visible to the decider.
- 2.4.1.1 S4 Every critical dependency confirmed with a fallback?: Fallback for every critical dependency.
- 2.5.1.1 S4 Run sensitivities: Top three sensitivities shown.

I'm the sponsor on {{initiative}}, working on step S5 "Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?" of the workflow "Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements".
The workflow's goal: Split the brief's value hypothesis into outcomes, give each a measured success criterion and write the business requirements that follow.

Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:

## What to do

2. Lay out each option with the evidence for and against it, the main risks, and your recommendation with reasons.
3. The options: Yes → continue to the next step; Disputed → re-split outcomes; Contradicts decision record → portfolio board.

## Apply
- Benefits realisation management — Plans, tracks and confirms the benefits an investment was made for, from the business case through to after delivery, so value is realised rather than assumed.
    How: Identify the benefits and their measures in the business case → Assign a benefit owner for each → Baseline and track the measures after delivery → Reconcile realised benefits with finance → Act on shortfalls and record the lessons

## Keep in mind
- Business / Strategy: Two to four criteria the sponsor will be judged on.

## Output
- A decision brief: the question, each option with evidence for and against, risks, and your recommendation — on one screen.

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] The options, evidence and recommendation are clear enough for me to decide in minutes

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.

files.title: Workflow 2.1.1.1 · Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements
files.body:
---
description: "Workflow — Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements"
argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Follow AGENTS.md. Log what you do in PROGRESS.md and register new IDs in TRACE.md.
Load these skills if you can: goal-tree, impact-mapping, five-whys, planguage, benefits-realisation-management.
Run it as specified in `workflows/plan-2-1-1-1-outcomes.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the product manager on {{initiative}}. I'm working on workflow 2.1.1.1: Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements.
Goal: Split the brief's value hypothesis into outcomes, give each a measured success criterion and write the business requirements that follow.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Opportunity brief
- Discovery decision record
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Opportunity brief accepted
- Sponsor available

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Read the brief & conditions aloud (Product manager)  [if: Brief conditions failed → back to DISCOVER]
- S2. Split the objective into outcomes (Product manager) → Outcome list
- S3. Pull baselines & set criteria (Data analyst) → Baseline data extract  [if: No data source → add a measurement requirement]
- S4. Draft business requirements (Business analyst) → Business requirements specification
- S5. ◆ DECISION — Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria? (Sponsor)  [if: Disputed → re-split outcomes; Contradicts decision record → portfolio board]
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Brief already carries criteria; No data source for a criterion.

- S4. Separate constraints & merge duplicates (Architect) → Constraint & assumption log  [if: Conflicts with a constraint → architect]

- Requirement classification — Sort each requirement into Functional, Business, UX or Non-functional; the classes are categories, never hierarchy levels.
- Requirements management tool — Holds requirements with IDs, classes, versions, trace links and change history.

- Quality attribute scenarios — A six-part way of stating a quality requirement so it is testable: source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.
- Planguage — A notation for stating quality requirements with a scale, a meter and target levels so they can be measured.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (requirement quality characteristics) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering.

## Keep in mind
- Requirements: One behaviour per requirement.
- Engineering: No implementation in requirement text.
- Data: Name the data each requirement reads and writes.
- Performance: Latency with a percentile and a load.
- Reliability / Resilience: Availability window and fallback behaviour.
- AI / ML: Extraction accuracy measured on a labelled test set, including poor scans.
- Security: Data stays in the EU tenancy.
- Privacy: Retention of order PDFs stated.
- Operations: Alerts and support hours stated.
- Accessibility: Highlighting distinguishable without colour alone.
- Architecture: ERP import API only stays a constraint, not a requirement.
- Quality / Testing: Could a test pass or fail on it?

## Rules
- Rework: Fails the quality check → rewrite

## If it goes off the happy path
- Pass → hand off
- Fail → rewrite
- No number → TBD
- Conflict → architect
- Infeasible → stop

## Output
- Requirements specification — a table with columns: RQ ID | Requirement (one behaviour or condition) | Class | Quality attribute (NFRs) | Measure & condition | Need | Horizon | Status
    (example row: RQ-001 | When a PDF order arrives in the orders mailbox, the system extracts the header and every order line | Functional | — | — | NEED-01 | Now | Reviewed)
- Quality-attribute drivers — a table with columns: ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic | Driver | Measure | Condition | RQ | Priority | Source

- ISO/IEC 25010 (product quality model) — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Quality attribute scenarios — A six-part way of stating a quality requirement so it is testable: source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.
- Requirements workshop — A facilitated session where stakeholders and the team discover and agree requirements together.
- Every requirement traces to a need — A requirement without a need is scope creep; a need without a requirement is a gap.
- Planguage — A notation for stating quality requirements with a scale, a meter and target levels so they can be measured.
- Requirement classification — Sort each requirement into Functional, Business, UX or Non-functional; the classes are categories, never hierarchy levels.
- Use cases — Describe how an actor achieves a goal with the system, step by step, including alternative and failure flows.

- Requirements (required)
- Engineering (required)
- Architecture (required)
- Concern: Untestable requirements
- Concern: Missing NFRs that surface later as incidents
- Constraint: ERP import API only
- Constraint: Engineering's ability to quantify

- One behaviour per requirement
- No requirement without a source need
- NFRs reviewed by engineering, security and operations

I'm the product manager on {{initiative}}. I'm working on subprocess 2.1.4: Trace, Validate & Baseline.
Goal: Prove the requirement set is right and complete enough for the next horizon, then put it under change control.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Requirements specification
- Stakeholder needs register
- Opportunity brief
- {{anything else relevant}}

- Requirements review passed

## What to do
Run this subprocess end to end with me, one workflow at a time, in this order:
- 2.1.4.1 Trace & Baseline Requirements — gate: Requirements baseline
    produces: Traceability matrix, Requirements baseline, Open questions log
- 2.1.4.2 Handle a Requirement Change — gate: Change decided
    produces: Requirement change request, Requirements baseline
- In parallel: Traceability build ∥ stakeholder walkthroughs
After each workflow, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate workflow prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Requirements Baseline review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- BABOK (requirements life cycle management) — The Business Analysis Body of Knowledge: six knowledge areas that describe how analysts plan, elicit, analyse, manage and validate requirements.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (requirements management and traceability) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering.
- Rolling-wave planning — Plan the near term in detail and the further term coarsely, then re-plan in waves as the horizon approaches and evidence arrives.
- Requirements baselining — Approving and versioning an agreed set of requirements as the reference point that later changes are measured from.
- Requirements change control — Every change to a baselined requirement is requested, analysed for impact and decided by the right person.
- Just enough, just in time — Detail work only as far as the next decision needs, and only when it needs it.
- Requirements traceability — Linking each requirement to its source and to what satisfies and verifies it, in both directions.
- Traceability matrix — A table linking each requirement to its stories, criteria, test cases and latest results, so coverage gaps are visible.
- Scenario walkthrough — Walk stakeholders through realistic scenarios to check the requirements cover what really happens.
- Requirements management tool — Holds requirements with IDs, classes, versions, trace links and change history.

- Requirements (required)
- Product (required)
- Customer / User (required)
- Concern: Baselines that freeze guesses
- Concern: Untraced scope
- Constraint: Next horizon only

## Rules
- Baselined requirements change only through change control
- Later-horizon items are not baselined
- Baseline versioned in the requirements tool

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Gaps found → back to Specify or Elicit
- A different valid path appears → Light profile: feature-level baseline kept in the backlog tool
- It goes beyond my authority → Unowned TBD on a now-horizon item → sponsor
- It should stop → Validation shows the outcomes can't be met → stop and return to DISCOVER — recorded in the learning log

I'm the product manager on {{initiative}}. I'm working on process 2.1: Requirements Engineering.

I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Opportunity brief
- Discovery decision record
- Stakeholder map
- Constraint & assumption log
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Opportunity brief accepted from DISCOVER
- Sponsor and stakeholders available

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 2.1.1 Derive Business Requirements & Outcomes — gate: Outcomes Agreed
    produces: Outcome & success-criteria map, Business requirements specification
- 2.1.2 Elicit Stakeholder & User Needs — gate: Needs Validated
    produces: Stakeholder needs register
- 2.1.3 Specify Functional & Non-Functional Requirements — gate: Requirements Review
    produces: Requirements specification, Quality-attribute drivers
- 2.1.4 Trace, Validate & Baseline — gate: Requirements Baseline
    produces: Traceability matrix, Requirements baseline, Open questions log, Requirement change request
- In parallel: Elicitation with different groups runs in parallel
- In parallel: NFR quantification ∥ functional drafting
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Requirements Baseline review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- BABOK — The Business Analysis Body of Knowledge: six knowledge areas that describe how analysts plan, elicit, analyse, manage and validate requirements.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering.
- ISO/IEC 25010 — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Quality attribute scenarios — A six-part way of stating a quality requirement so it is testable: source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.
- Requirements workshop — A facilitated session where stakeholders and the team discover and agree requirements together.
- Requirements baselining — Approving and versioning an agreed set of requirements as the reference point that later changes are measured from.
- Every requirement traces to a need — A requirement without a need is scope creep; a need without a requirement is a gap.
- Just enough, just in time — Detail work only as far as the next decision needs, and only when it needs it.
- Impact mapping — A mind map from a goal to the actors who can affect it, the impacts we want on their behaviour, and the deliverables that might cause them.
- Planguage — A notation for stating quality requirements with a scale, a meter and target levels so they can be measured.

## Keep in mind
- Requirements (required)
- Product (required)
- Business / Strategy (required)
- Engineering (required)
- Concern: Ambiguous or untestable requirements
- Concern: Missing NFRs
- Concern: Silent stakeholders
- Constraint: ERP import API only
- Constraint: Baseline only the next horizon

## Rules
- No requirement without a source need
- Constraints kept separate from requirements
- Change after baseline only through change control
- Requirements stored and versioned in the requirements tool

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Gaps found at validation → back to Elicit or Specify
- A different valid path appears → Light: feature-level baseline in the backlog tool
- It goes beyond my authority → Conflicting needs or unowned TBDs → sponsor
- It should stop → Outcomes can't be met or the brief's conditions failed → return to DISCOVER — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Outcome & success-criteria map — a table with columns: SC ID | Outcome (what a named role experiences differently) | Metric | Direction | Baseline | Target | Source | By | Brief clause | Benefit owner
    (example row: SC-1 | Clerks get an emailed order into the ERP quickly | Order-handling time per email order | Decrease | 14 min | 8 min | ERP timestamps (received → order saved) | 2025-09-30 | BRF-012 §3 | COO)
- Business requirements specification — a document with these sections:
    - 1. Business purpose and scope: Why the business is investing, in one paragraph, citing the brief.
    - 2. Outcomes and success criteria: Link to the outcome map — SC IDs only.
    - 3. Business requirements: One per line: ID · statement · SC served · source.
    - 4. Business rules and policies: Rules the solution must respect.
    - 5. Constraints: Limits on how — not requirements.
    - 6. Assumptions and open questions: With owners.
- Stakeholder needs register — a table with columns: Need ID | Stakeholder group | Need (their words, solution-free) | Outcome | Source | Kind | Validated by | Status
    (example row: NEED-01 | Order clerks | Get an emailed order into the ERP without re-typing it | SC-1, SC-3 | SES-07; workshop 17 Apr | Capability | Clerk lead Rotterdam | Validated)
- Requirements specification — a table with columns: RQ ID | Requirement (one behaviour or condition) | Class | Quality attribute (NFRs) | Measure & condition | Need | Horizon | Status
    (example row: RQ-001 | When a PDF order arrives in the orders mailbox, the system extracts the header and every order line | Functional | — | — | NEED-01 | Now | Reviewed)
- Traceability matrix — a table with columns: Requirement | Story | Criterion | Test cases | Latest run | Result | Gap?
    (example row: RQ-04 | STY-118 | AC-1 | TC-118-01, TC-118-02 | TR-0412 | Pass | ☐)
- Requirements baseline — a document with these sections:
    - 1. What is baselined: Horizon and requirement IDs in this version.
    - 2. What is deliberately not baselined: Next and later horizons stay coarse.
    - 3. Traceability: Link to the matrix and its completeness.
    - 4. Open questions: Each TBD with owner and date.
    - 5. Change control: How changes are requested and who decides.

## Before you finish, check

- [ ] Every NFR quantified against a quality attribute
- [ ] Bidirectional trace for the now horizon
- [ ] Requirements baseline approved and versioned
- [ ] Every now-horizon requirement traced to a need and an outcome

Goal: Map the journey, draw the smallest end-to-end slice that tests the value hypothesis, and publish what's in, out and later.

## Context I'm attaching
- Requirements baseline

- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Map the journey as a story map (Product trio) → Story map
- S2. Draw the MVP line (Product manager) → MVP definition
- S3. List in / out / later with reasons (Product manager) → In / out / later list  [if: Overlap with another initiative → portfolio board]
- S4. ◆ DECISION — MVP tests the hypothesis end to end? (Sponsor)  [if: Not end to end → redraw; No viable MVP → business case]
- S5. Publish the scope statement (Product manager) → Scope statement
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Dependency blocks the obvious MVP; Regulatory minimum.
If it fails: Redraw across the whole journey, thinner; Ask what the keenest stakeholder would add — and write it as out.

## Apply
- User story mapping — Lay the user's journey left to right, stories under each step, and draw release lines across to find a thin end-to-end MVP.
- Whiteboard — A shared physical or digital canvas for mapping, clustering and diagramming together.
- Lean Startup (MVP) — Build–measure–learn: test the riskiest assumption with the smallest experiment, then persevere or pivot.
- Walking skeleton — The thinnest possible implementation that runs end to end through every major component, built first to prove the path.
- Outcomes over output — Measure success by changed behaviour or value delivered, not by features shipped.
- MoSCoW — Sorts items into Must, Should, Could and Won't to set priorities and an explicit out-of-scope.
- Kano analysis — Classifies features by how their presence or absence affects satisfaction.
- Impact mapping — A mind map from a goal to the actors who can affect it, the impacts we want on their behaviour, and the deliverables that might cause them.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (scope and boundaries) — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering.
- Backlog tool — Holds the portfolio, product and iteration backlogs as linked items so every story traces up to its initiative.

## Keep in mind
- Customer / User: Map the clerk's real journey, email to ERP.
- Domain / Business Process: Include exceptions — unknown customers, partial orders.
- Product: Smallest slice that tests the value hypothesis.
- Engineering: Thin but end to end.
- Business / Strategy: Every out item has a reason the sponsor accepts.
- Finance / Commercial: Price each addition the sponsor asks for.
- Product: Does the MVP test the hypothesis?
- Requirements: In-scope items trace to the baseline.

## Rules
- Rework: Not end to end → redraw the line

## If it goes off the happy path
- Yes → publish
- Not end to end → redraw
- Overlap → portfolio board
- No viable MVP → stop

## Output
- Story map — columns:  | Receive email | Read order | Check & fix | Send to ERP | Measure
- Scope statement — a document with these sections:
    - 1. MVP and the hypothesis it tests: The smallest end-to-end slice and the result that would prove value.
    - 2. In scope: Traced to baselined requirements.
    - 3. Later (with trigger): What comes next and what releases it.
    - 4. Out of scope (with reasons): Explicit, with why.
    - 5. Constraints on scope: What limits the boundary.

files.title: Guardrails & hooks
files.body:
# Guardrails & hooks — Plan

People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.

## Always
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.
- Never paste passwords, keys, or personal data you aren't allowed to share — anonymise first
- At enterprise scale, use only approved tools
- Check every fact, number and source the agent gives you
- Agents prepare decisions; people make them
- Save the output in the artifact template and note that an agent helped
- If the agent's output is wrong, correct the prompt or the context — then record what you learned

## Scale: Solo / small
- Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.
- Watch for: Skipping discovery because 'I already know'
- Watch for: Accepting agent output unreviewed because there's no one else to check it

## Hooks — automatic where your agent supports them, a checklist everywhere else
| When | Check | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| Before saving an artifact | It follows its template · it carries its trace ID and links upstream IDs · every claim cites evidence or is marked 'Assumption:' · no personal data or secrets | Fix, or stop and tell me |
| Before a decision step | Stop. Prepare the decision brief. Wait for the named decision-maker | Never decide or approve |
| Before anything leaves the team | Messages, posts, invitations and shared documents are drafts until a person sends them | Ask for approval |
| Before using a new tool or data source | Is it allowed at this scale? Is the data allowed in this tool? | Ask first |
| After each step | Append to PROGRESS.md: date, unit, what was done, artifacts, decisions, open questions, next | Always |

## Rules and policies by unit
### PLAN
- No DESIGN or BUILD spend without a commitment record
- Baselined requirements change only through change control
- Quality is never the variable that gives
- Investment thresholds and delegated authority
- Incremental funding against evidence
- Funding envelope and delegated authority
- Team capacity
- Vendor connector by June
- Peak-season change freeze

### 2.1 Requirements Engineering

files.title: How to use this kit
files.body:
# Node agent kit — Plan

A ready project folder for running this act with your agent. People drive, decide and sign off; agents help.

## What's inside
- **Context file** — `AGENTS.md`: What the agent always knows about the initiative: how we work, the lifecycle, conventions, trace IDs, templates, ground rules and scale.
- **Skills** — `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: Reusable how-to packages — one per technique or method — with steps, structure, output templates and checks. The agent loads one when the task needs it.
- **Commands** — `commands/<name>.md`: Saved prompts you run by name, with arguments — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act.
- **Workflows** — `workflows/<name>.md`: A run specification: steps in order, inputs and outputs as files, who owns each step, human checkpoints, decision branches, recovery and the gate.
- **Subagents** — `agents/<name>.md`: Specialised helpers with one job — lens reviewers (privacy, security, finance…), a researcher, a synthesiser, a challenger, a decision-brief writer.
- **Tools & connectors** — `TOOLS.md`: Which tools and data each step needs — web search, documents, spreadsheets, the backlog tool, the research repository, the code repository — and what each scale allows the agent to do with them.
- **Guardrails & hooks** — `GUARDRAILS.md`: Rules the agent must follow and automatic checks at key moments — before saving an artifact, before a decision, before sending anything outside the team.
- **Rubrics** — `rubrics/<artifact>.md`: A scored checklist for each artifact, from its template, quality criteria and the unit's criteria.
- **Memory & handoff** — `PROGRESS.md · TRACE.md · docs/`: What carries across sessions and people: the project folder, a progress log, and a trace-ID register.
- **Templates** — `templates/`: the artifact templates the work produces.

## Set it up
1. Put this folder at the root of your project repository or shared drive and fill `{{initiative}}` in AGENTS.md.
2. Point your agent at it — how each layer is picked up:
   - Context file: Many coding agents read AGENTS.md at the repository root. Tools with their own file (e.g. CLAUDE.md) can import or copy it. In chat assistants, paste it into the project's instructions.
   - Skills: Agents that support skills load SKILL.md folders from their skills directory. Otherwise attach the SKILL.md as a file, or paste it before the prompt.
   - Commands: Agents with custom commands or saved prompts read Markdown files from their commands / prompts folder; $ARGUMENTS takes what you type after the name. Otherwise paste the file.
   - Workflows: Point the agent at the workflow file ("run workflows/x.md, stop at every checkpoint"). Orchestration tools can execute the YAML block; people can read it as a checklist.
   - Subagents: Agents that support subagents load them from their agents folder. Otherwise open a separate conversation and paste the file as its first message.
   - Tools & connectors: Connect tools through your agent's connectors or MCP servers; grant the least access the step needs.
   - Guardrails & hooks: Agents with hooks can run these checks automatically; everywhere else they're a checklist the agent applies and you confirm.
   - Rubrics: Any agent: "score docs/x.md against rubrics/x.md".
   - Memory & handoff: Keep them in the repository or shared drive the agent can read; start each session with "read PROGRESS.md".
3. Start with the command `plan-run-act`, or the command for the unit you're on.
4. After every step: check the output, score it against its rubric, save it in `docs/`, and log it in PROGRESS.md.

Tools change quickly — check your agent's documentation for where it reads context files, skills, commands and subagents.

_Practice_ — A regular session where the product owner, trio and delivery team split, clarify and estimate upcoming items so they become ready.

Weekly, about 10% of the team's time.

4. Estimate

# Benefits realisation management

_Framework_ — Plans, tracks and confirms the benefits an investment was made for, from the business case through to after delivery, so value is realised rather than assumed.

Every initiative with a value hypothesis — measured after release, not just at the business case.

# Multi-level backlog

_Pattern_ — Keeps work in linked backlogs at different sizes and horizons — initiatives, epics and features, stories — each owned and refined at its own cadence, so strategy traces down to the sprint and evidence traces back up.

## When to use it
Any organisation running more than one team or initiative.

## How to do it
1. Portfolio backlog: initiatives, ranked quarterly by the portfolio board
2. Product backlog: epics and features, ordered by the product owner
3. Iteration backlog: stories pulled into a sprint by the team
4. Link every item to its parent
5. Detail just in time — the further out, the coarser

## Structure
- **Portfolio backlog** — Initiatives · quarters · portfolio board
  - **Product backlog** — Epics → features · months · product owner

---
name: risk-register
description: "A living list of risks with owner, rating and treatment, kept current as work proceeds. Use when from discovery onward. In Node: 2.5.3.1 S1 Refresh the risk register."
---

# Risk register

_Pattern_ — A living list of risks with owner, rating and treatment, kept current as work proceeds.

## When to use it
From discovery onward.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.5.3.1 S1 Refresh the risk register — command `plan-2-5-3-1-s1-refresh-the-risk-register`

## How to do it
1. Add each identified risk with its cause
2. Rate likelihood and impact
3. Assign an owner and a treatment
4. Review at each gate; close or update

## Structure
| ID | Risk | Cause | Likelihood | Impact | Rating | Owner | Treatment | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 |  |  | 1–5 | 1–5 | L × I |  | Avoid / reduce / share / accept | Open |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Risk register → `templates/risk-register.md`, saved as `docs/risk-register.md`

## Quality checks
- Risk register: Every risk owned
- Risk register: Rated against appetite
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

files.title: Rolling-wave planning
files.body:
---
name: rolling-wave-planning
description: "Plan the near term in detail and the further term coarsely, then re-plan in waves as the horizon approaches and evidence arrives. Use when baselining, reconciling and roadmapping in PLAN. In Node: 2.1.4.1 S3 Mark horizons & log open questions; 2.3.4.1 S5 Update backlog & re-forecast; 2.4.2.1 S3 Overlay dependencies & forecast."
---

# Rolling-wave planning

_Practice_ — Plan the near term in detail and the further term coarsely, then re-plan in waves as the horizon approaches and evidence arrives.

## When to use it
Baselining, reconciling and roadmapping in PLAN.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.1.4.1 S3 Mark horizons & log open questions — command `plan-2-1-4-1-s3-mark-horizons-and-log-open-questions`
- 2.3.4.1 S5 Update backlog & re-forecast — command `plan-2-3-4-1-s4-update-backlog-and-re-forecast`
- 2.4.2.1 S3 Overlay dependencies & forecast — command `plan-2-4-2-1-s3-overlay-dependencies-and-forecast`

## How to do it
1. Detail the next horizon only
2. Keep later horizons as outcomes and T-shirt sizes
3. At each wave, detail the next horizon from what was learned

## Structure
- **Now** — Requirements baselined, slices sized, dates forecast
  - **Next** — Features and coarse sizes
    - **Later** — Outcomes and problems only

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Open questions log → `templates/open-questions.md`, saved as `docs/open-questions.md`
- Delivery forecast → `templates/delivery-forecast.md`, saved as `docs/delivery-forecast.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Never re-planning the later waves
- Open questions log: Every TBD owned and dated
- Open questions log: Blockers flagged
- Delivery forecast: 50% and 85% dates
- Delivery forecast: Assumptions listed
- Delivery forecast: Re-forecast every sprint
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
PMI; common agile planning practice

files.body:
---
name: sensitivity-analysis
description: "Change one input at a time to see how much it moves the result, and so which assumptions matter most. Use when forecasts and business cases. In Node: 2.3.3.1 S3 Read 50% / 85% dates & assumptions; 2.3.4.1 S2 Generate & cost options; 2.5.1.1 S4 Run sensitivities."
---

# Sensitivity analysis

_Technique_ — Change one input at a time to see how much it moves the result, and so which assumptions matter most.

## When to use it
Forecasts and business cases.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.3.3.1 S3 Read 50% / 85% dates & assumptions — command `plan-2-3-3-1-s3-read-50-85-dates-and-assumptions`
- 2.3.4.1 S2 Generate & cost options — command `plan-2-3-4-1-s2-generate-and-cost-options`
- 2.5.1.1 S4 Run sensitivities — command `plan-2-5-1-1-s4-run-sensitivities`

## How to do it
1. List the main inputs
2. Move each by a plausible range
3. Rank by effect on the result

## Structure
| Input | Change | Effect on NPV |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minutes saved per order | ±30% | ±€0.40M |
| Rollout speed | −3 months | −€0.16M |
| Licence cost | +50% | −€0.02M |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Forecast assumptions → `templates/delivery-forecast.md`, saved as `docs/delivery-forecast.md`
- Trade-off options → `templates/tradeoff-record.md`, saved as `docs/tradeoff-record.md`
- Sensitivity analysis → `templates/benefits-model.md`, saved as `docs/benefits-model.md`

## Quality checks
- Forecast assumptions: 50% and 85% dates
- Forecast assumptions: Assumptions listed
- Forecast assumptions: Re-forecast every sprint
- Trade-off options: At least three options
- Trade-off options: Quality never the variable
- Trade-off options: Rejected options kept
- Sensitivity analysis: Low / likely / high
- Sensitivity analysis: Run cost included
- Sensitivity analysis: Sensitivities on the top drivers
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

files.body:
---
name: spike
description: "A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question. Use when when feasibility depends on an unknown. In Node: 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton; 2.3.1.1 S3 Size later items by T-shirt."
---

# Spike

_Pattern_ — A short, timeboxed piece of throwaway work that answers one specific technical question.

## When to use it
When feasibility depends on an unknown.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton — command `plan-2-2-3-1-s1-choose-the-walking-skeleton`
- 2.3.1.1 S3 Size later items by T-shirt — command `plan-2-3-1-1-s3-size-later-items-by-t-shirt`

## How to do it
1. Write the single question
2. Set a strict timebox
3. Build only enough to answer it
4. Record the answer and the decision; discard the code

## Structure
- **Question:** One question, answerable yes / no or with a number
- **Timebox:** e.g. 2 days
- **Approach:** What will be tried
- **Result:** What was found
- **Decision:** What this changes

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Walking skeleton → `templates/slice-plan.md`, saved as `docs/slice-plan.md`
- Estimate sheet → `templates/estimate-sheet.md`, saved as `docs/estimate-sheet.md`

## Quality checks
- Walking skeleton: Skeleton first
- Walking skeleton: Each slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small
- Walking skeleton: No layer slices
- Estimate sheet: Sized by the people who'll build it
- Estimate sheet: Uncertainty recorded
- Estimate sheet: Never converted into hours
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

files.title: Stage-gate
files.body:
---
name: stage-gate
description: "Divides work into stages separated by gates. Use when for investment decisions that need explicit, auditable checkpoints — in Node, initiative-level decisions. Inside a funded product, the Definition of Ready and Done replace heavy gates. In Node: 2.5.2.1 S1 Split into evidence-gated tranches; 2.5.4.1 S2 Run the commitment meeting; 2.5.4.2 S5 Update the portfolio register."
---

# Stage-gate

_Framework_ — Divides work into stages separated by gates. At each gate a decision-maker reviews the evidence against criteria and decides whether work continues.

## When to use it
For investment decisions that need explicit, auditable checkpoints — in Node, initiative-level decisions. Inside a funded product, the Definition of Ready and Done replace heavy gates.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.5.2.1 S1 Split into evidence-gated tranches — command `plan-2-5-2-1-s1-split-into-evidence-gated-tranches`
- 2.5.4.1 S2 Run the commitment meeting — command `plan-2-5-4-1-s2-run-the-commitment-meeting`
- 2.5.4.2 S5 Update the portfolio register — command `plan-2-5-4-2-s4-update-the-portfolio-register`

## How to do it
1. Define stages and what each must produce
2. Define gate criteria in advance
3. At the gate, review deliverables against the criteria
4. Decide: Go, Kill, Hold or Recycle — and record why

## Structure
1. Stage: do the work
2. Gate: review evidence
3. Go / Kill / Hold / Recycle
4. Next stage

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Tranche plan → `templates/funding-request.md`, saved as `docs/funding-request.md`
- Portfolio backlog entry → `templates/portfolio-backlog.md`, saved as `docs/portfolio-backlog.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Gates that never kill anything
- Avoid: Gates that become bureaucracy without evidence
- Avoid: Gating every feature — use it for investments, agile cadences for the work inside them
- Tranche plan: Tranches tied to evidence
- Tranche plan: Authority level stated
- Portfolio backlog entry: Every initiative links to its decision record
- Portfolio backlog entry: Ranked by value, cost of delay and size
- Portfolio backlog entry: Active initiatives limited
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Robert G. Cooper (Agile–Stage-Gate hybrid: Cooper & Sommer, 2016)

files.title: Stakeholder onion
files.body:
---
name: stakeholder-onion
description: "A concentric diagram placing the solution at the centre and stakeholders in rings by how directly they are affected. Use when at the start of discovery to make sure nobody affected is missed. In Node: 2.1.2.1 S1 Plan elicitation per group."
---

# Stakeholder onion

_Pattern_ — A concentric diagram placing the solution at the centre and stakeholders in rings by how directly they are affected.

## When to use it
At the start of discovery to make sure nobody affected is missed.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.1.2.1 S1 Plan elicitation per group — command `plan-2-1-2-1-s1-plan-elicitation-per-group`

## How to do it
1. Put the product or change at the centre
2. Add the people who operate or use it directly
3. Add the containing business — managers, sponsors, other teams
4. Add the wider environment — regulators, partners, the public
5. Check each ring for missing groups

## Structure
- **Wider environment** — Regulators, partners, competitors, public
  - **Containing business** — Sponsor, managers, other departments
    - **Operational users** — People who use or run it day to day
      - **The solution** — The product, process or change

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Elicitation plan → `templates/elicitation-plan.md`, saved as `docs/elicitation-plan.md`

## Quality checks
- Elicitation plan: Every group in the stakeholder map has a row
- Elicitation plan: Negative questions planned
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Ian Alexander, stakeholder analysis

---
name: story-splitting-patterns
description: "Named ways to split a large item into smaller valuable ones. Use when slicing features. In Node: 2.2.3.1 S2 Split each feature by pattern."
---

# Story splitting patterns

_Method_ — Named ways to split a large item into smaller valuable ones.

## When to use it
Slicing features.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.2.3.1 S2 Split each feature by pattern — command `plan-2-2-3-1-s2-split-each-feature-by-pattern`

## How to do it
1. Try workflow steps
2. Try business-rule variations
3. Try data variations
4. Try happy path then unhappy paths
5. Try a spike to remove uncertainty
6. Check each result is still valuable

## Structure
| Pattern | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Workflow steps | Read → review → send |
| Business-rule variation | Known vs unknown customer |
| Data variation | Top-20 layouts vs any layout |
| Happy / unhappy path | Clean PDF first, then poor scans |
| Spike | Can poor scans be read at all? |

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Slice plan → `templates/slice-plan.md`, saved as `docs/slice-plan.md`

## Quality checks
- Slice plan: Skeleton first
- Slice plan: Each slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small
- Slice plan: No layer slices
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Richard Lawrence, Humanizing Work

Defining the MVP.

# Vendor due diligence

_Practice_ — Checking a vendor's viability, security, data handling, service levels and exit before depending on it.

## When to use it
Before committing to a vendor dependency.

Applied in Node at:

## How to do it

2. Review security certification
3. Confirm data residency
4. Check SLA and support
5. Plan the exit
6. Test their claims on your data

- **Security:** …
- **Data residency:** …
- **SLA:** …
- **Exit plan:** …
- **Claims tested:** …

files.title: Vertical slicing
files.body:
---
name: vertical-slicing
description: "Cutting work so each piece cuts through every layer and delivers a behaviour someone notices, rather than a layer. Use when decomposing features and slicing stories. In Node: 2.2.2.1 S2 Split epics into features; 2.2.3.1 S2 Split each feature by pattern."
---

# Vertical slicing

_Pattern_ — Cutting work so each piece cuts through every layer and delivers a behaviour someone notices, rather than a layer.

## When to use it
Decomposing features and slicing stories.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.2.2.1 S2 Split epics into features — command `plan-2-2-2-1-s2-split-epics-into-features`
- 2.2.3.1 S2 Split each feature by pattern — command `plan-2-2-3-1-s2-split-each-feature-by-pattern`

## How to do it
1. Name a behaviour a user notices
2. Include every layer it needs
3. Put technical work under it as tasks

## Structure
**Do**
- 'Clerk sees low-confidence fields highlighted'

**Don't**
- 'Back end: confidence service' as its own item

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- Feature → `templates/product-backlog.md`, saved as `docs/product-backlog.md`
- Slice plan → `templates/slice-plan.md`, saved as `docs/slice-plan.md`

## Quality checks
- Feature: Every item traces to an initiative, problem or improvement
- Feature: Ordered — no two items share a rank
- Feature: Only the next 1–2 quarters detailed
- Slice plan: Skeleton first
- Slice plan: Each slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small
- Slice plan: No layer slices
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Common agile practice

description: "The thinnest possible implementation that runs end to end through every major component, built first to prove the path. Use when the first slice of a new system or integration. In Node: 2.2.1.1 S2 Draw the MVP line; 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton."

# Walking skeleton

_Pattern_ — The thinnest possible implementation that runs end to end through every major component, built first to prove the path.

## When to use it
The first slice of a new system or integration.

Applied in Node at:

- 2.2.3.1 S1 Choose the walking skeleton — command `plan-2-2-3-1-s1-choose-the-walking-skeleton`

## How to do it
1. Pick one simple case
2. Make it flow through every component end to end
3. Deploy it
4. Thicken it slice by slice

## Structure
1. Email in
2. Read one PDF
3. Draft in ERP
4. Measure

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- MVP definition → `templates/scope-statement.md`, saved as `docs/scope-statement.md`
- Walking skeleton → `templates/slice-plan.md`, saved as `docs/slice-plan.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: Building one layer fully before connecting the rest
- MVP definition: MVP is end to end
- MVP definition: Every out item has a reason
- Walking skeleton: Skeleton first
- Walking skeleton: Each slice valuable, demonstrable, testable, small
- Walking skeleton: No layer slices

Alistair Cockburn

# Weighted scoring

_Method_ — Scores options against weighted criteria so trade-offs are explicit and comparable.

## When to use it
Value rating and decision packs.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.5.4.1 S1 Assemble the commitment pack — command `plan-2-5-4-1-s1-assemble-the-commitment-pack`

## How to do it
1. Choose criteria
2. Weight them (sum to 100%)
3. Score each option 1–5
4. Multiply and sum

## Structure
| Criterion | Weight | Score (1–5) | Weighted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User value | 30% |  |  |
| Business value | 30% |  |  |
| Effort (inverse) | 20% |  |  |
| Risk (inverse) | 20% |  |  |
| Total | 100% |  | Σ |

## Output
Write results with these templates:

files.title: WSJF
files.body:
---
name: wsjf
description: "Weighted Shortest Job First: rank work by cost of delay divided by job size, so the most valuable small items go first. Use when ranking initiatives in the portfolio backlog and large features in the product backlog. In Node: 2.2.4.1 S2 Apply job size & compute WSJF."
---

# WSJF

_Technique_ — Weighted Shortest Job First: rank work by cost of delay divided by job size, so the most valuable small items go first.

## When to use it
Ranking initiatives in the portfolio backlog and large features in the product backlog.

Applied in Node at:
- 2.2.4.1 S2 Apply job size & compute WSJF — command `plan-2-2-4-1-s2-apply-job-size-and-compute-wsjf`

## How to do it
1. Estimate cost of delay (value + time criticality + risk reduction)
2. Estimate job size
3. Divide and rank

## Structure
> WSJF = cost of delay ÷ job size → highest first.

## Output
Write results with these templates:
- WSJF scoring sheet → `templates/wsjf-sheet.md`, saved as `docs/wsjf-sheet.md`

## Quality checks
- Avoid: False precision — use relative scales
- WSJF scoring sheet: Relative scale
- WSJF scoring sheet: Scored by a group
- WSJF scoring sheet: Rationale per row
- Every claim cites evidence or is marked "Assumption:"

## Source
Don Reinertsen; SAFe

# Feasibility assessment — {initiative}

- **Initiative:** 
- **Owner:** 
- **Version:** 
- **Status: Draft / In review / Approved:** 
- **Last updated:** 

## Rating
_High / medium / low feasibility, in one line._
> Example: Medium — import is proven; parsing accuracy is the open risk.


## Unknowns and how they were resolved
_Table: unknown · spiked? · finding · impact._
> Example: ERP throughput — spiked — 1,800/h — resolved.


## Quality attributes at risk
_From ISO/IEC 25010._
> Example: Reliability of parsing on poor scans.


## Skills and capacity
_What's needed vs available._
> Example: Needs 1 ML-capable engineer for 2 months.


## Conditions
_What must be true for the rating to hold._
> Example: Vendor X confirms ERP connector by June.


## Sign-off
- Engineering lead: ____________  Date: ______

- **Owner:** 
- **Version:**

## Problem statement
_Who has what problem, in what context, with what impact. No solution words._
> Example: Order clerks in the EU unit spend ~2.5 hours a day re-typing emailed PDF orders into the ERP, delaying confirmations and causing picking errors.


## Who
_The users and segments affected._
> Example: 8 order clerks across 2 sites.


## Impact
_Why it matters — to users and the business._
> Example: ~20 h/day of manual work; 3% order error rate.


## Primary job
_The main job story._
> Example: When a customer emails an order PDF, I want it in the ERP without re-typing, so I can confirm the same morning.


## Evidence
_Link to the evidence trace._
> Example: 6 sessions; 2-week inbox sample (1,140 orders).

_The smallest end-to-end slice and the result that would prove value._
> Example: Rotterdam clerks import clean PDF orders from the top 20 customers without re-typing. We're right if handling time at Rotterdam is ≤ 10 min within 4 weeks.


## 2. In scope
_Traced to baselined requirements._
> Example: RQ-001–003, RQ-006–009 at Rotterdam.

> Example: Faxed orders — under 2% of volume. Auto-posting without review — trust not yet earned. Customer order portal — separate initiative.

files.title: Workflow 2.1.1.1 · Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements
files.body:
# Workflow 2.1.1.1 · Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements

Split the brief's value hypothesis into outcomes, give each a measured success criterion and write the business requirements that follow.

**Run it:** ask your agent to "run `workflows/plan-2-1-1-1-outcomes.md` for {{initiative}}, stopping at every checkpoint", or use the command `plan-2-1-1-1-run-outcomes`. Each checkpoint means: show me the output and wait. At `decision` checkpoints the named person decides.

```yaml
workflow: plan-2-1-1-1-outcomes
title: "Derive Outcomes & Business Requirements"
owner: "Product manager"
inputs:
  - "docs/opportunity-brief.md"
  - "docs/decision-record.md"
preconditions:
  - "Opportunity brief accepted"
  - "Sponsor available"
steps:
  - id: s1
    do: "Read the brief & conditions aloud"
    owner: "Product manager"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: plan-2-1-1-1-s1-read-the-brief-and-conditions-aloud
    reviewers: [business-reviewer]
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "Brief conditions failed → back to DISCOVER": stop
  - id: s2
    do: "Split the objective into outcomes"
    owner: "Product manager"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: plan-2-1-1-1-s2-split-the-objective-into-outcomes
    skills: [goal-tree, impact-mapping, five-whys]
    reviewers: [product-reviewer, customer-reviewer]
    output: "docs/outcome-map.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: s3
    do: "Pull baselines & set criteria"
    owner: "Data analyst"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: plan-2-1-1-1-s3-pull-baselines-and-set-criteria
    skills: [planguage]
    reviewers: [data-reviewer, finance-reviewer]
    output: "docs/baseline-extract.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
    on:
      "No data source → add a measurement requirement": s4
  - id: s4
    do: "Draft business requirements"
    owner: "Business analyst"
    agent: "draft, then wait for review"
    command: plan-2-1-1-1-s4-draft-business-requirements
    reviewers: [requirements-reviewer]
    output: "docs/brs.md"
    checkpoint: review-at-end
  - id: d1
    decision: "Sponsor agrees outcomes & criteria?"
    owner: "Sponsor"
    agent: "prepare a decision brief — never decide"
    checkpoint: decision   # stop; Sponsor decides
    branches:
      "yes": gate
      "Disputed → re-split outcomes": s2
      "Contradicts decision record → portfolio board": authority
gate: "Outcomes agreed"
criteria:
  - "Each criterion has direction, baseline, target and source"
checks:
  - "Baseline check against source data"
on_failure:
  - "Pull a two-week baseline sample before agreeing"
  - "Rewrite each outcome as a change a named role experiences"
rework: "Sponsor disputes an outcome → re-split and re-measure"
outputs:
  - "docs/outcome-map.md"
  - "docs/brs.md"
handoff: "Outcome & success-criteria map & BRS → 2.1.2 Elicit Stakeholder & User Needs"
learning:
  - "Criteria that later proved unmeasurable"
```

```yaml
orchestration: plan-2-1-1-outcomes
title: "Derive Business Requirements & Outcomes"
owner: "Product manager"
```
